newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's master of unity could be next PM.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's master of unity could be next PM.

text.p: Ivan Kostov, a vegetarian who likes to jog, wooed 15 fractious Bulgarian opposition parties into the coalition which forced the ruling ex-communists to quit this week and call elections.
Kostov, 47, is now odds-on favourite to become prime minister after early elections in April.
An associate professor of economics, he has served twice as finance minister since the fall of one-party communist rule in 1989 -- once in a 1990 caretaker government and then in 1991.
He is committed to economic reforms and says he would act quickly to implement them if the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) wins the general election.
"We have a clear programme for governing the country," said UDF deputy Asen Agov. "Returning (collectivised) land, a currency board, privatisation, a deep cut in red tape."
But Kostov would also push hard to advance Bulgaria's case for membership in the 15-nation European Union and the Western NATO military alliance.
The latter would clearly upset Moscow, which opposes NATO expansion and was a staunch ally of communist Bulgaria during the Cold War.
Some of the measures which a Kostov government would have to take would test his popularity with the crowds who have cheered him so far.
A plan for a "currency board" to stop the freefall of the lev, Bulgaria's currency, would put a stop to printing of money and could force deep jobs cuts, diplomats said.
But the alternative would be a worthless currency, losing value by the hour, and hyperinflation. Inflation has already hit 50 percent a month.
Kostov's friends say he would be a firm leader and that he gets angry when things do not go his way.
"He's easy to work with as long as you know he's in charge. He has a sense of humour, is polite with friends but he can be distant and cold with people he doesn't like," said one Kostov associate.
Clearly building his popular power base, he has turned out every day at mass demonstrations at Sofia's central Alexander Nevski Orthodox cathedral.
For 30 days, always donning a blue UDF headband, he ignored bouts of flu and freezing temperatures to address the rally with words of encouragement.

"For seven years my generation, and the one after it, have gone through the great drama of being unable to guarantee their children a normal life in their own country," he told a victory rally after the ex-communists gave up.
"We also felt humiliated, cheated and helpless until these 30 days which changed Bulgaria. Thank you for this solidarity, for this support which was for Bulgaria's future," he said.
At the victory rally Kostov playfully sprayed his followers on the cathedral steps with champagne, and then the throng of flag-waving supporters filling the square.
On other days he bounced up and down with the multitude when the battle cry "Communists Can't Jump" was raised.
Kostov's toughest task may be holding the disparate parties of the UDF together through the election campaign and trying to forge them into a united government.
"This victory did not decide our fight for democracy. It will be decided in April, when the democratic forces must win parliamentary elections at all costs," he told the rally.
Kostov was born in Sofia on December 23, 1949. He is married to Elena Grigorova and has two daughters.
